en: Table of Contents for the Recorded Sayings of Master Shu’an of Yunju:
The Record of the Yan-sheng Chan Monastery on Mount Zhang-xi in Qingyuan Prefecture.
Recorded Sayings of Zhēnrú Chan Monastery on Yúnjū Mountain in Nánkāng Commandery;
Verses and Eulogies Spoken While Dwelling in Dōnghú Lane;
Ancient Cases, Buddha and Patriarch Portraits, Hymns, and Gāthās.
The Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Shu’an of Yansheng Chan Monastery on Zhangxi Mountain in Qingyuan Prefecture,
compiled by his junior disciple Liaojian.
On the thirteenth day of the fourth month in the twelfth year of the Jiading era, he entered the monastery.
Pointing to the mountain gate:
entering directly and exiting directly; acting directly and employing directly. A fleeting turn at the profound pivot—hitting the mark every time, one hundred out of one hundred.
The Buddha Hall.
Pointing to the earth, pointing to the heavens; the grass-thief is utterly defeated. Entering the weeds to seek the man, he offers a mere three prostrations.
The Abbot occupies this chamber; there is nothing that can or cannot be done. When he wishes to walk, he walks; when he wishes to sit, he sits. The lacquer buckets press against one another.
All at once it was shattered. A three-legged toad penetrates the nine heavens; Mount Songshan’s Broken Oven-Fallen One laughs until he falls over.
On the Dharma-seat: one, two, three, four, five; six, seven, eight, nine, ten. Sitting and cutting off the crown of the head, a thousand sages cannot reach it.
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "A single cloud over Lake Hu takes the bright moon as its intimate friend. Yet it is blown by the pure wind, carried into the deep mountains.

Thus, meeting things, one immediately establishes the source; following conditions, one acts as the master. It reaches the point where the myriad phenomena intersect and the seven peaks bow their heads.
The mountain flowers offer smiles, and the mountain stream flows with a gurgling sound—this clearly reveals the true mechanism. One must strictly avoid [seeking it] amidst the weeds."
Setting foot down, with a single casual leap, he brushes past the great void. He casts his line into a ten-thousand-fathom abyss, yet stands alone atop the peaks of a thousand mountains.
This is still but the ordinary practice of a patch-robed monk. But tell me: what is the single phrase for reaching home without raising a blade?
Furthermore, how is it? "The signs of Great Peace appear as heaven and earth are still; the Imperial Way is impartial as sun and moon are bright.
At this late hour, for the evening *sǎn*, I break open the void until there is no seam; the patch-robed monks may enjoy this wherever they are.

Yet, because of the holy retreat (*shèngzhì*), we have entered the mountains and are dreaming north of the clouds and south of the clouds. Therefore, the Buddhas of the three periods and the patriarchs of successive generations throughout the world...
Old Monk: The mountains, rivers, and great earth; the sun, moon, and stars; the grasses, trees, insects, and creatures—each and every one is dreaming.
New Elder: Having recently departed from a famous mountain, you have come to roam these rocky valleys.

Holding your staff upside down and wearing your straw sandals backward, you have pierced through twenty li of clouds to laugh at the bright moon in the cave-heaven. Yet, you cannot avoid dreaming with your eyes wide open, thinking by day and dreaming by night.
Objects. Night-dreams and daytime thoughts are conditions; from kalpas past to this very day, there has never been a gateway [between them].
Now tell me: Are all phenomena dreams? What, then, are these phenomena? Or are phenomena not dreams? Where, then, do they reside within a dream?
It is like the reflections of various people appearing in a mirror: if one sets aside the mirror, what is the image? Directly and suddenly transcend the shadow.
An image—clearly knowing where it returns. It is like washing away soil with soil from within the mud.
When Chan Master Taibai suddenly heard of this, he could not help but laugh heartily, saying: "My dream has already awakened; yours is only now beginning. One awakens, one acts;
there is a call and a response. At midnight, the golden cock crows once, and all the confusion is rent asunder."

Ascending the hall for the Summer Retreat: Today we enter the retreat; every matter transcends the ordinary. Inquiring after one’s health and burning incense—this is the very core of the patch-robed monk.
In the sequence of human affairs, from high to low, as one proceeds through the halls in order, the True Person of No Rank suddenly lets out a sneeze. Why is it so?
The mouth of the cloth bag is tied; all is auspicious and nothing is not favorable.
Entering the hall, [the Master said]: "Zen Master Taibai was utterly without skill; with a single fly-staff he arrived, seizing the heights of a thousand peaks.
Using the central tree, he established a sacred image, mixing water with mud to grow roots from the soil. Without changing his bones or shedding his skin, he attained transformation."
There is no need to follow patterns or imitate models. This single segment of true body and mind has a ten-thousand-fathom halo behind the head.
When [Zhaozhou] asked for flour while ascending the hall, he recalled a monk visiting Master Guanzhuo. Guanzhuo took some flour and showed it to him, whereupon Zhaozhou composed a mountain verse.
Master Guanzhuo manifested great capacity on the spot; meeting people, he used his bare hands to uphold them. If you can directly realize the essential point, you will understand.
When the waves of the Buddha-ocean are inexhaustible, he ascended the hall.
He raised the following case: A monk asked Yunmen, "What is the place where all Buddhas emerge? Yunmen said, "Water walking on the mountain to the east.
He then offered this verse: Water walking on the mountain to the east; Qian-yuan, li, zhen, and heng. A single word is a source of confusion.
Talentful men vie with one another for the lead.
Entering the hall, [the Master] raised the following case: A monk asked Baizhang, "What is the extraordinary matter? Baizhang said, "Sitting alone on the Great Hero Peak. [The Master] commented:
"Baizhang was caught off guard by this monk’s question; he did not realize his hands were exposed and his feet were bare. Today, suddenly there is..."
When someone asked Zhàngxī, "What is the extraordinary matter? he replied to him: "The Patriarch left behind a lump of clay;
let those who eat it rest when they are full."

Ascending the hall on the Double Fifth: Today is precisely the Double Fifth Festival. For the patch-robed monk, there is a truly wondrous secret method for turning the holy into the mundane and transforming gold into iron.
Instead of bamboo leaves, he uses mountain tea; instead of glutinous rice dumplings, the plate is full; the calamus is finely sliced.

Even so, though worldly airs have not yet been removed, it is necessary for everyone to be warmed and refreshed. At this very moment, the hundred grasses— (Note: The text appears to be incomplete at the end.)
At the head of the hall, the person of mugwort is filled with joy; amidst the shadows of a thousand peaks, he laughs without ceasing. Wild monkeys occasionally tug at the wisteria vines.

Entering the hall during the midsummer retreat: the feet are neither fixed nor unfixed; the center is neither dwelt upon nor not dwelt upon. Coming and going without obstruction, he kicks and tramples the living void.
Shooting and killing the tiger of the South Mountain, he turns his body and draws the horned bow. Above, there is nothing to grasp or look up to; below, all is cut off.
One's own person: solitary and towering, not a single speck of dust stands; clear and vast, the eyes reach the end of a thousand peaks.
White clouds drift in flakes, flowing waters layer upon layer. Suddenly, the entire vessel is overturned, yet one must still call west east. Upon this lump of raw iron—
The fissures gape open; within the dried riverbed, the traces of fish are revealed. This is neither wondrous function nor supernatural power.
Everyone has no other business: the impartial Lord of the House. *Tut!* In old age, both ears have gone deaf.
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "To the south of Zhaozhou is the Stone Bridge; within the Guanyin Monastery dwells Maitreya.
The Patriarch left behind a single sandal, yet to this very day it cannot be found. Old Zhaozhou, with his hands, planted thorns and grew prickly ash by the gate.
No one from the four quarters enters; they merely frown in vain in the dark. O Great Assembly, if you wish to pass through Zhaozhou’s Barrier..."

Mo. At the moment of casually turning one's head—on the twenty-fifth day of the sixth month, ascending the hall—the World-Honored One held up a flower and Kāśyapa broke into a smile. This was simply because, in trying to imitate another's steps, he lost the way to Handan.
How can this compare to Seven Peaks today? He has cut down the tree before the courtyard and let forth the mountains beyond the clouds. Proceed!
As soon as a person blinks, their body is already within a painted scene. Where birds cannot fly, there is no climbing or reaching across time and eternity.
At such a moment, after the man of Dongting has departed, who can understand leaning against the balustrade?
On the fifth day of the seventh month, he ascended the hall. Drums were beaten and gongs struck as they vied to climb the pole.

How many people felt their hearts ache on level ground? The Seven Peaks have a method for finding a place of rest: with hands in sleeves and no words, watch from a cool distance. Watching is easy; climbing is difficult.
They drape the rope and ascend, crossing their bodies; they race along the flagpole. Suddenly, they turn around and perform a somersault. Just so!
At such a time, the Buddhas and Patriarchs appeared on the stage, each displaying their skillful hands and smiling; because of the plucking of the flower, they all fell into a leaky trap.
Dongshan’s “three pounds of flax,” Yunmen’s “dry dung pellet,” Deshan’s staff upon entering the gate, and Linji’s shout upon entering the gate—how could a mirage ever quench thirst?
Yet Zen monks have their own distinct regulations; today, before this assembly, I shall clear the matter once and for all.
The pearl is called "night-shining"; the sword is named "Great Void.
Upon ascending the hall at the conclusion of the summer retreat, he sought words: "In the immortal abode, many strange herbs grow; in the sacred ground, the tracks of the mundane are severed.

When the autumn wind stirs the scales and shells, the living snake transforms into a dragon. Is there anyone here who can summon clouds and spit forth mist? (The question and answer are not recorded. Ninth [Day] of the Summer Retreat.
Ten days have passed; the flavor within the quietude is long-lasting. It is fortunate that there is but a single plate of rice—what need is there for pepper and ginger?

Ascending the hall, he raises the story once more: snow upon snow, frost added to frost. If one is a connoisseur of flavor, even encountering the choice cuts from the imperial kitchen, how could they fail to swallow with appreciation?
If one has not yet known the flavor, upon merely seeing the butcher’s gate, they must surely feast with great gusto. The handle of the Seven Peaks ladle.
There are hands; they may add, and they may take away. At times it is clear and vast, with not a trace of speck or grain remaining;
at times it is thick and dripping, with all five flavors complete. Today, I have formed it into a single mass and, within this bottomless bowl, offer it universally to all.
Winter Solstice Small Sermon: Distinguishing the Seasons. Not a single thing is in opposition; everyone extends their hand, each one upholding it.
White rice cakes are sliced into pieces and pounded hard; wild fruits, large and small, are served as appropriate. For us monks, our teeth are like sword-trees and our mouths like dragon-pools.
Once they enter the teeth and bite down, they spit out a misty spray of saliva. Suddenly, they collide with the thorny *liji* (the "thorn-bush" kōan).

One can only frown in the dark; cast away upon a heap of refuse, the thousand sages have never known its whereabouts. At the point where Dongshan shifts his perspective, the opportunity before one’s eyes is lost. At this very moment, when things are thus, one receives blessings in accordance with the time. How would you say it? "At midnight, the mass of darkness is completely incinerated; a single sprout of Yang blazes forth on the southern branch. Forcefully speaking of a single thing to expose the family's disgrace, he draws onlookers to take their seats. With a smile, he lightly shifts the entire tray;
the Seven Peaks stand towering as the Three Terraces dance.

The next day, he ascended the hall: "Clear skies on the Winter Solstice—auspicious and favorable in every way. Whether sitting, reclining, walking, burning incense, or sweeping the ground, this is the eye of the Patriarchs and the very core of the monks.
Throughout the eight seasons and four times of the year, each remains in its proper place. (He held up his whisk and said: "The whisk nods its head;
joyfully and happily, one wanders freely in the celestial caverns. Rejoicing at the arrival of this season, the Way of the Gentleman flourishes."
The petty person avoids it; with time, it grows by a single thread. Do not waste the passing moments; hold fast to heaven and earth.
Upon what principle does this rest? Beneath the foundation stone lies hidden gold; at Fengcheng, the spirit of the sword is buried.

On the day the Buddha attained enlightenment, he ascended the hall; because he awakened to the Way upon seeing the morning star, he could not avoid casting his entire body into the grass, thereby bringing trouble upon his descendants for generations to come.
He instead took the appearance of a layman and dyed it white. If Seven Peaks had seen him on that day, he would have struck him down with a single blow to the face.
Why was this so? Though it be a good cause, it brings about an evil fruit.
Ascending the hall on New Year’s Eve: Seven Peaks has nothing with which to celebrate the year. He shakes out his many years of livelihood;
the whisk wags its tail and shakes its head, performing the lion’s playful dance. With a casual roar, he makes heaven and earth tremble.
In the eastern village, the old man burns paper money throughout the night; the deity of the earthen stove dares not doze. Amidst the sound of crackling firecrackers, I offer this verse:
At the end of the year, there is nothing to extend our greetings. The four walls are deeply enclosed, and smoke fills the house.
How many times have I pushed it aside only to ask myself: When the firewood is exhausted, that is the New Year.

On the first day of the New Year, he ascended the hall: "The beginning of the year opens a new reign; all things are renewed. Without the need for deliberation or conjecture, one encounters the body of total reality.

Even reaching this point, one must still advance further, turning over upon the tip of the whisk. Now tell me: how do you speak the single phrase of 'receiving blessings in accordance with the season'?
Within the brazier, cold ashes once again send forth flames; In the mountains, withered trees are entirely reborn in spring.

Ascending the hall on the fifth day of the first month: "The moon does not exceed five; today it has arrived in person. Knowing the time and recognizing the season, he accords with circumstances and cherishes the Way.

He does not speak of the upward-trending vehicle of the patriarchs, nor does he cast aside the secret signals of Dongshan. When the incense pillar and the lantern collide, they encounter one another and laugh aloud.
But tell me, what is it that they laugh at? Han Xin releases the iron falcon. [This concludes] the verse on Baizhang’s Wild Fox.
A story. Baizhang and the Wild Fox. The barren woman has no husband; once her tears fall, the vast ocean dries up. Administrative Assistant Xie Xin returns to the Treasury Office;
Administrative Assistant Hui enters the monastery to arrange offerings. Holding up his seven-strip robe, he ascends the hall.
After the three rounds of drums have ceased, the Elder ascends the hall. The two classes of officials question Xie, while the Attendant burns incense. Before he has even opened his mouth, each...

Each raises it up. The Way enters through faith; faith is able to uphold and direct. Using the long to cultivate the short, using the short to follow the long—when a guest arrives from beyond the clouds, one sets forth offerings to satisfy their parched gut.
With ample room for maneuver, there is something else to deliberate.
But tell me, what is it you are deliberating? Once you have grasped it with a confident hand in the darkness, you will win a hearty laugh.
Yunmen held up [a case] where he asked a monk: "Why do you put on your *kāṣāya* when you hear the sound of the bell? He composed a verse, saying:
"The bell sounds and the *uttarāsaṅga* is donned; Taken at hand, it requires no effort. How laughable is that Elder Ming of old, Hurrying and chasing about in such a frantic rush."

Having taken up the *kāṣāya*, he ascended the hall the following day to express his gratitude: "Having taken up the *kāṣāya*, I rejoice in its lightness and ease; a single sheet of idle cloud wraps around half my shoulder.
Do not be surprised that I shake it frequently when meeting people; I borrow my neighbor’s skirt to bow for my neighbor’s New Year.
If you can see it here, then repaying kindness and returning virtue will be fully accomplished. If this is not yet so, it will be difficult upon the *pāṇḍava* stone.
Lifting it up: he makes the man who was treading the mortar in years past laugh to his downfall.
Entering the hall on a snowy day: "Last night at the upper hall, the incense-chamber was opened; at dawn, they ate snow-balls in the refectory.
Picking them up with his hand, he hurls them right in one's face; who knows who recognizes the coldness of this act for others?"

Ascending the hall, he said: "The spring snow melts and the spring waters swell; the spring breeze blows up clouds from the celestial caverns. Falling plum blossoms pierce through the green of the moss.
Words are uttered yet are not sound; form precedes things. The eyes are revealed at the tips of the hundred grasses;
one probes for the bone within the void. The monks in the forest delight in non-action; at dawn they sing a song of Great Peace. What is this Great Peace?"
Píngqū. We meet at the start of the new year; I humbly wish you ten thousand blessings.

Today, the twenty-fifth day of the second month, the Abbot of Tiānbái Ān, Tánjiān, has requested me to ascend the seat for the hundred-day memorial service of his late teacher, the Administrative Head Cáijǐ.

At this moment, I have casually drawn a crossbow capable of launching a thousand-jìn bolt, and with a single arrow, I have struck the red heart. Across the great earth, there is not an inch [of space left].
The earth—surrounded on all four sides and above and below, with no barriers or screens—is laid bare, revealing the master within the White Star Hermitage.
Last year, because he returned from the funeral of his original teacher, he could not help but cry out "Injustice! at every sound. Amidst suffering there is joy; amidst joy there is suffering.
With a shout, he drove away the old hag of Ciming. He moved from the inauspicious to the auspicious and changed his grave site. At such a time as this, tell me: where is Administrator Cai?
In this place, the flowing waters of the southern stream are as blue as a conch shell; dwelling deep amidst falling blossoms, they are like a rain of red.
The countenance of the former master remains solemnly present; entrust it to Old Jian, who shall receive and preserve it.
As the assembly concluded their session, the Abbot said, "Venerable Jian-si Cai, is this life or is it death? Listen once more to this verse:
To fully understand that life and death are fundamentally the same— Countless deep reds interspersed with pale reds. How laughable that the patch-robed monk has no use for them;
He has given his robes and bowl entirely to the spring breeze."
On the eighth day of the fourth month, he ascended the hall: "In the toil of life, one is in deep slumber; yet at the break of dawn, one has already set out.

Upon reaching home, this one decisive stroke—the sun rises and affairs arise once more. Had one encountered someone of such natural magnanimity at that moment, they would have driven away the nine dragons and kicked over the perfumed waters, sparing us from this mutual dullness.
Today, following the perverse and pursuing the evil, you head toward the Great Hall."
[The Master] poured three ladles of water with great care directly onto his head.
He then ascended the hall and said: "Today is the tenth day of the fourth month; the patch-robed monk walks alone and stands apart. In a casual glance, he turns the profound pivot."
Crushing empty space to extract its essence; leaping and bounding within flashes of lightning; appearing and disappearing amidst motes of dust;
a hundred paces before a precipitous cliff, each step naturally higher than the last. The distance from head to tail is not much at all;
a black steed from a thousand miles away cannot catch up.
Ascending the hall for the commencement of the retreat. (He draws forth the "Bag of Joy. The sacred regulation has arrived; the Seven Peaks have established their camp.

With the six sense-faculties as the gateways and the single thought-moment as the commander-in-chief, one must not let anything go out within nor allow anything to enter from without. One should settle oneself firmly upon the meditation mat.
On the meditation cushion, the two sides spar; once the battle-weary struggle is complete, there is no passing through the boundaries.
Even if Deshan’s staff falls like raindrops and Linji’s shout rushes like thunder, when one reaches this point, seeing the strange as not strange, the strangeness vanishes of its own accord.
Planning from within the tent, one relies on it to secure victory. The bag of joy is opened amidst laughter; the treasure within the robe is grasped with庆快 (joyful ease). No longer...

Circumambulate the long corridors; there is no need to go from room to room for trade. A decoction of mugwort shall suffice for the ritual; everyone should perform three prostrations with unopened sitting cloths.

Ascend to the hall. Last night there was nothing to do; at dawn, it is announced that we shall ascend to the hall. It is fortunate indeed to have this single bowl of rice; what need is there for other grains?
Ginger from the square plot. Although it is thus, coarse food satisfies easily, while chewing delicately makes one hard to hunger.
[The Master] ascends the hall: "The Buddhas of the three periods do not know that there is; the mad Puhua performs somersaults. The cat and the white ox, however, do know that there is;
when Han and Shi meet, they open their smiling mouths. The jackal howls, yet it is the lion’s roar. Eight taels and half a catty."
Ten *shuan* make one *dou*. Do not seek it from others; you must return to what is of your own. What is the news of that which belongs to oneself?
A dog does not choose its home based on poverty; a child does not disdain its mother for being ugly. This is a verse on the story of the "Cypress Tree.
Zhaozhou’s courtyard cypress—when explained to Zen guests—it is a commodity at its true price, and the coins must be full in their count.

Ascending the hall, [the Master] raised an ancient case: A monk asked Mazu, “What is the Buddha? Mazu said, “The very mind is the Buddha. The monk asked, “What is the Way? Mazu said, “No-mind is the Way.
The monk asked, “How far apart are the Buddha and the Way? Mazu replied, “The Buddha is like an open hand; the Way is like a clenched fist.”
Master Mazu has cast everything forth before all of you. Should this not yet be clear, listen further to this verse:
The Buddha is like an outstretched hand; the Way is like a clenched fist. Fully upholding the true command, it is without faction or partiality.
In the eye of a gnat, a night market is set up; upon the tongue of a tiger, one swings on a swing.
The Summer Retreat Concludes; Ascent to the Hall. Before the fifteenth day is the binding; after the fifteenth day is the releasing.

Binding is appropriate; releasing is appropriate. With eyes open or closed, legs extended or drawn in—Buddhas and Patriarchs act like compassionate mothers, administering medicine according to the ailment.
Now the true essence is perfectly at ease; medicine and illness are swept away all at once.

Bare and empty, stripped of all possession, one lets out a long whistle beneath the moon and before the wind, startling the thousand-year-old crane atop the pine branch. The crane stumbles; the wind blows through the corner of the hall, shaking the bells.

Ascending the hall, he said: "To speak from the Dharma seat is easy; to speak by the brazier is difficult. To speak before awakening is easy;
to speak after awakening is difficult. Yet it is neither difficult nor easy—it is like the *Shennong Bencao* (Shennong’s Herbal Classic) or the *Maha Baiji* (The Hundred Taboos)."
Ascending the hall, he said: "Last night I heard the plum blossoms outside the window scolding the peach blossoms, saying: 'I alone possess the height of spring; I am celebrated by many poets.
I secretly reveal my sandalwood heart, my entire being pure and clear. You do not know that there is ice and snow in the human world.
The peach blossoms then scolded the plum blossoms, saying: 'I sway the spring light; my flowers bloom in profusion. Yet you remain silent, with not a single word. He then descended from his seat.
It forms a path. You know only the spotless white; how can it compare to my crimson, as bright as the midday sun? Suspecting that winter flowers have suddenly appeared, I advise you:
"The red is naturally red, and the white is naturally white. Whether red or white, there is no need for nine hundred."
When the abbot heard of this, he could not let it pass. "The peach is red and the plum is white; my ear is on one side.
Unable to bear that these winter flowers had appeared so pointlessly, he forcibly urged [the guest] and struck him with thirty blows of his staff. But tell me, where did the fault lie?
Last night the east wind secretly drew forth the twigs; two leaves are like a donkey’s ears. Entering the hall [he said]:
"How extraordinary! How extraordinary! Living in this little hut, one can truly enjoy oneself. Two children suddenly begin to fight; few know of the fall in between.
What is the message for those who do know? One need only worry about riding a horse.
[He was] slippery. Thus he made his way back by boat.
Upon ascending the hall, he met Master Fozhao and asked about his original face. Day after day he sought a response; night after night he pondered it thoroughly.
He exhausted every skill and artifice for exactly a year and a half, yet even until now, thirty years later, when has he ever [attained it]?
I saw it in a dream. [The Master] ascended the hall and said: "The ancients said: 'For over thirty years I have dwelt at Zihu; my strength has been sufficient for the morning and evening gruel.
When there is nothing to do, I go up the mountain for a stroll. I ask you, people of this time: do you understand? The ancients only knew how to shut their doors and practice within."
The carriage cannot leave the gate, for its tracks have merged; for over thirty years I have dwelt in a thatched hut. Within the hut there is nothing with which to engage in inquiry.
Sometimes I go north, south, east, or west; speaking in plain vernacular, I am idle, clamorous, and unrestrainedly foolish.
Ascending the hall, he said: "Dwelling in this hermitage, it stands solitary and remote. The embers in the brazier are as if entirely extinguished. In vain one sends children to gather dry firewood;
yet, picking up whatever comes to hand, one finds a single piece. One strikes it and blows upon it—the light is bright and pure.

Warmth fills the entire body, and heat pervades the whole house. Blazing and surging, there is no door through which to rest. At nightfall, it lies in disarray, burning people's clothes. Thus, it is casually brought forth."
The Seal for Settling the Fire: Pointing with one's finger at the tip of the firewood, it is said, "Hook it in a place beyond doubt.

Ascending the Hall: When entering the mountains to dwell in a hermitage, one’s whole body is amidst the wild weeds; foxes and badgers intertwine their tails. At the head of the hut, the spirits cry out in pursuit;
those who hear this are chilled to the core, and those who see it give rise to affliction. I have a method for settling the mind: release Han Xin.
Iron Hawk. Ascending the hall, he said:
"I have a fire attendant who is very clever at his work. Having eaten his fill, he takes up his hoe and goes to the hermitage to hoe the earth, leaving not a trace of a blade of grass behind.
He knows no taboo regarding good or evil. Now tell me: when the earthworm is cut into two pieces, how many worms are there?"
Both heads move; in which head does Buddha-nature reside? *Suru-siri*. Ascending the hall, she said:
"I am naturally ashamed of my many flaws and clumsiness; I see the snow piled high upon my head. In spring, I long to marry once more;
I beg the Lord of the East to act as my matchmaker. I shall take empty space as my bridal curtain And take the great earth as my wedding procession."

Her adornments are such: she takes the snow for her topknot, the moon for her comb, the mountains for her hairpins, the waters for her sash, the willows for her brows, and the peach blossoms for her cheeks.
She is most elegantly refined and possesses an air of transcendent grace. Now tell me: how would you express it in a single phrase upon her departure?
"A fresh breeze rises at dawn; A plum blossom dots the gray moss like a face in bloom."
Ascending the hall, he said: "In the corners of the eaves, mountain flowers bloom profusely; amidst the groves, the spring colors are mild and warm.

Everywhere children gather ferns; in abundance, secluded birds build their nests. The Patriarch’s intent from the West has left no trace; yet at the treetops, the hundred-tongued thrush still speaks much."
Ascending the hall, he said: "A few pieces of yam roasted by the embers, Two or three thatched huts nestled beside the woods.
If a practitioner wishes to come and visit, I shall surely be in a hurry to drive them out of the mountains."

Ascending the hall: On this New Year's Eve, there is nothing to distribute for the year’s end; we merely burn some wood chips in the incense burner. The stench of the smoke strikes right into our nostrils.
A sudden sneeze clears the fever from one’s face; the dull lethargy of the year’s end is here dispelled. From this point on, the Buddha-dharma of the new year shall be auspicious.
But tell me: how would you express the first phrase of this connection? "The sound of the crackling firecrackers reaches the ears, and the children rejoice."
The spring breeze passes in secret; the grasses and trees know it.

Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "Today is the first day of the first month. All matters are auspicious from the very beginning. The harmonious atmosphere is warm as spring; the flavors of the world are sweet as honey.
The sun and moon come and go in turn; time and light do not fail one another. How can one speak a single phrase that does not involve the myriad conditions?"
A discourse. Throughout the year of three hundred and sixty days, I have been ascending the hall.
Since spring came, I have unconsciously experienced what was like a dream: I dreamed that the kingdom of Campā and the kingdom of Silla were contending for the forehead [in a wrestling match].
When the Great Image of Jiazhou turned its head to look, it crushed Mount Sumeru, such that the heavens, the earth, and the great world were utterly overturned.
Sentient and insentient beings were all shaken at once. Upon waking from the dream, it was realized that it had originally been the pillow falling to the ground and the urinal being broken.
Now tell me: when Yangshan pushed out the pillow, Guishan said, "To employ matters of the sword’s edge is already to wound one's own blade and offend one's hands.
Today, with the pillow falling to the ground, even the bystanders cannot help but laugh until they fall over.

Ascending the hall: This morning is the fifteenth day of the first month; all things are renewed. For a patch-robed monk who possesses not a single thing, what object could one offer with such earnest devotion?
The silver candle shines brightly like the moon in the heavens; the flower of the lamp blooms throughout the spring within the cave. At this very moment—
The beggars of the East Street were fighting with the beggars of the West Street.

Just as the *Sumeru Lamp* was about to intervene to mediate, it was struck by a single blow and fell straight down three feet into the earth. The lantern and the pillar heard this suddenly in the dark and could not help but laugh heartily.
But tell me, what were they laughing at? "Had I known earlier that the lamp was fire, the rice would have been cooked long ago."
After a long time, he ascended the hall.

"The monk’s family understands their own spiritual nature; they possess the capacity for transformation and the skill to respond to circumstances. Since the world has already become turbid, one cannot claim to be pure oneself.
Since the world has already fallen into intoxication, one cannot claim to be sober oneself. One must move in harmony with the light and blend with the dust. [He] turned his head...
The head is already fully realized. Have you not seen it? Long ago, the Grand Marshal Dang, though lacking discernment and clarity, was nonetheless distinct and clear.
When the plum blossoms fell, he ascended the hall and seized the very essence of the scene: at the end, the flowers bloom, falling in profusion like snow upon the gray moss.
Where the fragrant scent wafts, there is much of the real; within that reality lies the talent to season the imperial cauldron. As soon as the sprout emerges, one sees what is within.
O Benevolent One, what serves as proof? When green, it bites; when wrinkled, the brow furrows. Once ripe, the yellow plum is passed on at midnight.
A verse on the ancient case of the dog having no Buddha-nature.
In vain I have used light ink to paint these weeping willows; their supple branches stretch a hundred feet long. I send this word to the traveler:
do not look at them. To gaze upon them even once is enough to break one’s heart.
The attendant reports that the Great King Zhaozhou has arrived;
the old shoes’ laces have snapped and their tongues have opened. Buried beneath the bed, they are covered in dust. Picking them up with a casual hand, he puts them on;
before the crowd, he drags them back and forth.
The void dissolves as the sun sets;
today, with high honors, he returns from the imperial examination. Wild flowers and singing birds all welcome and follow him. His mother-given countenance is exactly as it was before;
only his green cassock differs from times past.

Transcending the four propositions and severing the hundred negations, pale reds and deep greens swirl in dense confusion. Here, at every house, bamboo gates stand open. How lamentable are those who come and go for sightseeing;
they do not realize their own bodies have already passed through the Flower Village.
Bimā grasps her staff;
at the head of the swift rapids she holds her fishing rod. The vast waves surge as the evening river grows cold. Even the glistening scales understand how to follow the hook upward;
with a single gulp, the blue sea is drained to its very bottom.

Not a companion to the myriad dharmas, he seeks laughter and mirth in the wind, smiling amidst frost and ice. He reveals the springtime light and lets forth its fragrance. Across the two banks, the broken bridge is crossed by no one;
throughout the river, sparse shadows stretch across the slanting sun.
When one who has undergone the great death returns to life, what then? Night travel is forbidden; at dawn you must arrive.
Once we have met face-to-face, there shall be no more concealment. Just look into this ancient mirror upon the stand: it reflects you in the dark and reflects me as well.
A single expanse of clear light, its brilliance chilling to the bone.
For thirty years, Mazu has lacked salt and sauce;
this beggar has neither thread nor rags. He carries stale rice and leftover gruel upon his shoulder, and lifts up his many-year-old tattered straw mat;
before others, he feels no shame or embarrassment.
Yangshan pushed out his pillow;
even the "Water Ox" is worthy of praise. Having snapped the nose-rope, he lies amidst the mists and clouds.
Suddenly, lightly scratching where it itches, he immediately reveals his tail before people.
Do not obscure the person of original nature; I ask the Master to cast his eyes high. Look directly down:
the momentum of the strange rain and wild wind is about to topple all; the dark clouds hang over the six directions as they surge upward.
A single cascade falls before the cliff, cleaving through thousands of layers of green mountains.

Eating oil-cakes on high, the foul mouth opens and reveals the thief’s body; look, he stirs up dust upon level ground. Those who watch from the sidelines do not understand how to keep their tongues hidden;
they too become people whose teeth are smeared with sticky paste.
Daowu said: "I will not speak of life; I will not speak of death.
He casts forth the luminous pearl, its brilliance shimmering; he cleaves the fine jade, leaving no trace. Several times he offered it for sale, but no one would buy;
alas, the beggar laughs at how he has failed to repay this kindness.
Niaokuo blows on a tuft of cloth;
blood splatters within the weeds. He casually unbinds the head of a venomous serpent. Blazing, malevolent winds strike against the heavens;
in the midst of the scorching sun, mirages form like towers.
The story of Shoushan’s bamboo whisk overturns the mountains;
the iron ball on the red furnace is perfectly round. Gently nudging it, one’s very bones and hair turn cold;
its crimson light penetrates straight through the azure heavens, filling the valleys and gullies with nowhere to rest.
From the southern peak of Xuefeng, the turtle-nosed snake leaps forth—the turtle-nosed snake of the southern peak!
It leads idle fellows to compete in following the heterodox. Amidst a throng of ten thousand people, it bites over one’s shoulder;
only a true child recognizes the father.

Hiding one's body within the Northern Dipper, one lightly tosses a brick amidst the bustle. The nostrils of all patch-robed monks are pierced at once. Having laughed until the heavens tremble, he returns;
striking the south, the north is moved.
Nanquan’s Beheading of the Cat is but ordinary daily fare; when guests are invited to stay, the etiquette is relaxed.
Yet for those who have already eaten their fill at Shangfang, even if the entire platter were presented before them, they would be unable to eat.
Zhaozhou wears straw sandals upon his head;
the young prodigal loves tattooing his skin. His patterns and his flesh reflect each other in brilliance.
Amidst the clamor, he seeks only to hide his vulgar eyes, yet he arrogantly takes this nakedness as his glory.
The cypress tree before the courtyard gate is like a single strand of oil-silk floating upon the water’s surface. Swaying with the waves, it drifts along with the current;
casually cast into the rivers and lakes, it catches a golden-scale fish and refuses to let go.
The Three Sages come forth whenever they meet people; Xinghua does not come forth when meeting people, yet he has seized the essential core of the Great Master.
He spreads his mats before the gate and opens his shop at will; in the end, the滞貨 (stale goods) are traded in the marketplace with fellow merchants.
Whether the price is high or low, neither side disputes it.
A monk asked the Sixth Patriarch, "Who has attained the essential meaning of Huangmei? The Patriarch replied, "The person who understands the Dharma has attained it.
The monk asked, "Has the Master attained it? The Patriarch said, "I do not understand the Buddha-dharma.
Looking up, all is vast and silent; there is not a single speck of dust. In my old age, I have no place to settle my body. I have already endured many cycles of snow and frost."
"Bitter! To speak of willow blossoms brings grief that kills a man.
Muzhou said, "This is a settled case; I grant you thirty blows.
Sailing against the current past the Haimen Gate, where the sky is shrouded in a dense, dark mist. Lift your head and you shall see the Fusang tree immediately."
Guo said, "Do not fix the compass needle to distinguish dawn.
Purin Gongfeng annotated the sutra; the National Teacher showed him a cup of water, seven grains of rice, and a pair of chopsticks.
The willows form layers of lush, verdant clusters. The three paths open wide without any winding turns. Before the gate is simply that which was there before;
it is entrusted to Yuanming to "Return Home."
Ding Shangzuo saw Linji seize him and give him a slap; Ding bowed and suddenly attained realization.
The fire-seed in the firewood suddenly blazed red; amidst the wild grass heap, a swift wind struck, so that the gnat in the eye could find no place to rest.
Mooring here, she unleashes a fierce blaze that freely consumes the void.

When examining the old woman’s words, the old woman appears destitute and lonely, as if seeking a husband; when Zhaozhou hears this, he immediately establishes a kinship. Upon returning, he speaks only of affection and gratitude.
Talk. How laughable that you have needlessly invited the dust of worldly defilement!
When Luzu saw a monk, he faced the wall;

skulls lie scattered across the wilds, impossible to conceal. Obstructing the traveler in the cold, it only becomes more apparent as it hangs down. From this point on, examine and verify with a single glance.
Afterwards, one must also bury it deeply in the crude ground.
When Lingyun saw the peach blossoms, Xuansha said, "He has not yet reached the ultimate.
Lingyun saw them once and had no further doubts; if he had not reached the ultimate, to whom would he have clearly explained it? To pile more manure upon a heap of broken wine-jars.
[Earth-Emperor]. Blowing with the wind, blowing against the wind.
It is so, yet it is also not so. Peach blossoms open, apricot blossoms open; a lingering fragrant breeze strikes the nose. All that falls away follows the flowing water.
Depart! Not a single speck of green moss remains.

Begging for alms while discussing the burning of paper—pointlessly inviting malevolent spirits. Look, look! The household ghosts have returned to bring calamity; they play at the gate under the blue sky and bright sun.
The door: closing it with the back of the hand and opening it with the palm facing forward.

Washing the bowl, he speaks of the desolate village where nothing exists to be elegant. Not knowing how to adorn herself, she knows no shame; amidst the weeds there is a flower, which she picks up as she goes.
Broken. It is casually stuck in the head of a rustic.
When Zhaozhou visited the two hermits, Tianxiong’s aconite came from Mianzhou;
whether the price was high or low, it was paid at the same rate. Whether curing illness or killing people, it depends on what is required.
In the end, it is difficult to find its trace.
Because students ask, "When birth and death arrive, how can one withstand them? the Master replies with four verses:
"When birth and death arrive, how can one withstand them? A stone man suddenly develops a sore upon his head. As soon as this itching spot is scratched..."
Having donned [his robes], he stepped before the people as Meng Bala.
When birth and death arrive, what can one withstand? When a beggar meets another, he empties his bag at once. Looking around in all directions, there is nothing at all;
it is laughable that this single body has nowhere to hide.
When birth and death arrive, what can one withstand? Returning in solitude, the path is grand and clear.
I send this phrase of "arriving home" as a brief message, inscribing it into the ranks of wild geese across the azure sky.
When birth and death arrive, what can one resist? Under the bright moon on a quiet night, we deliberate together. The lotus flower and its leaves convey the message:
when a breeze comes, there is a fragrance.
The Buddha and the Patriarchs praise the image of leaving the mountains:
eyes cold as if containing frost, ears adorned with rings; head and face covered in wild, mottled grass. With the arrival of spring, it blooms once more.
Green. When did Laozi ever leave the mountains?
Above, not a single tile; below, not a single awl. This solitary, impoverished body is known only to himself.
From this point on, entering the stream wherever he dwells, he carries a live fish in his hand.
Vimalakīrti holds a fly-whisk in his hand and sits upon a low stool; his eyes are like shooting stars and his hair like hoarfrost.
He opens the gate of non-duality yet constantly feigns illness, effectively gouging healthy flesh to create a sore.
Bodhidharma was once involved in the smuggling of private salt; without cause, he crossed the border and ran into the King of Liang. Without even being interrogated, he was defeated;

his tracks were left in disarray at the official marketplace, leading people to laugh and marvel at him. His carrying pole was stripped of both ends, and to this day, it has been entirely without sale.
Master Pang gained an advantage, yet it was a loss of advantage. He exhausted his family treasures to sell a colander;
his sons and daughters huddle together with no fruit to show. Such a father-in-law is truly ignorant.
The Patriarch’s seal-stamp defiles the idle paper and ink of the human world. Because of that paper, five leaves and one flower bloom. Behold them as they pass down the fragrance in succession;
all have come from imitating the gait of Handan.

Hanshan and Shide—when Hanshan and Shide meet, they clap each other on the shoulder. Both gathering and both releasing, they overturn the heavens. Throughout antiquity and today, it is one vast field of leisure;
it reveals itself within the ordinary realm of tea and incense.

In the Diagram of the Three Teachings, six ears do not share a single plan. Looking at one another, they have already leaked the secret; in the end, there are only three people. To verify a tortoise, one ends up with a soft-shelled turtle.

"It is," "it is," "this," "that"—non-action and quiescent extinction. The way to nourish the family is the same, yet the paths taken are each different. Are they different or not? They dangle [the hook].
A blow from the staff knocks down the moon at the edge of the sky.

Contemplating the flowing water, Avalokiteśvara—a sheet of cold spring water comes splashing against one’s face. On the precipice of a steep cliff, it is as slippery as moss. Raising one's head, one simply follows the current.
Water. When did the Great Being ever have his eyes opened wide?
Chan Master Yantou and Layman Ganqi dwelling together in a layperson’s house is utterly lacking in decorum.
Black and white are distinct, yet they appear as if not aligned; you vainly expose the needle before others.
A thread. He profits from women and couples.

The eyes in the bag are as cold as the moon over a thousand rivers; his brows span ten thousand layered mountains. With a staff over his shoulder, he carries a cloth bag, walking wherever his feet lead him through the human world.
The shrimp leaps out from the mortar; held fast in his hand, it does not enter the mud and water, and thus loses its life.
A verse:

Song of the Final Hermitage: A three-bay thatched hut is fit for spending one's final years; A simple life, lived as it may, is sufficient and good. The moon-lake faces the door, its mirror-light cold;
The bamboo path winds around the eaves, leading to the Great Way. The wind blows, leaf after leaf, naturally forming a heap; Picking them up with my hand as they come— one [after another].
The stalk of grass is as base as mud, yet as precious as a jewel. When needed, it is used without seeking; the nostrils of the vast sky have been pierced by it.
Travelers passing by are all brought low. A-he-he! Do you understand? Go ask Zhang Siguo of the village ahead.
The icchantika sings of non-abiding and non-attachment; an old dhyāna-demon who rejoices in little but possesses much malice. Within the flowers of the three poisons he binds bitter fruits;
within a garden of thorns he nurtures a honeycomb. He speaks of harmonizing Samantabhadra while selling white elephants; he calls out to children to fill the Yellow River.

He plays with the tiger of the Southern Mountains; he tramples the surging waves of the Northern Sea. He washes away the grievances of Buddhas and Patriarchs; the war-drums and spears of the Dharma-battle have ceased.
The five thousand words are wiped clean like a rag; the assembly on Vulture Peak is but a basket of refuse.

In vain he utters meaningless speech, singing the song of the icchantika. The melody is archaic and unfit for hearing, yet its resonance penetrates to the very depths of the crags. It is wondrously subtle and utterly transcendent.

Touching and rubbing, one draws the thread from within the six sense-faculties; amidst the flash of lightning, one thrusts the shuttle. Thus is woven the seamless robe, and embroidered are the bottomless boots.
When the dance of the Three Terraces concludes, there is a hearty laugh—a laugh that topples the many years of the black old woman.
The Song of the Straw Sandals:
The people of the village know its intent; Woven by hand, it is most easily made. Its length and size are right before one's eyes;
With diligent effort, it is swift and effective. Leaping out from within the grassy thicket, One ties the knot at the end with a firm grip.
The nose is firmly bound and tucked tight against the ears; cast upon the ground, it makes a golden sound. Raising his steps, he leaves the mud and water behind;
he enters into a thousand mountains and ten thousand peaks. Grasping both the head and the tail of his feet, Zhaozhou exerts all his strength but cannot lift them up.
Xuansha is caught in the snare and kicks his own toe. Dragged here and there, the head passes through; lightly tossed into the filth.
Song of the Cane Staff: The cane staff is most transcendent; From beginning to end, its black scales are cracked and weathered. A chilling wind arises, as firm as iron;
It travels with me and rests with me. It moves freely at will, trailing and dragging along; It stirs the dragons in the azure depths, And strikes down the heavens.
The crescent moon sometimes reaches the summit of a thousand peaks; the thousand peaks and ten thousand crags all burst asunder.
At other times, it plunges people into the wild weeds, its hidden traces difficult to discern. The plantain tree has suffered a wrong for which no one clears the injustice;
Da sui raises it up, yet it leaks heavily. Now that I am old and weary, I lack the strength to support it; I snap it with my hand, and it becomes two pieces.

Clarifying the fundamental principle, the ancient path is overgrown with moss and the way has already gone astray. Upon rootless trees, empty flowers bloom; when a single flower falls, it becomes an empty fruit.
Picked up at random by hand, it is but a bitter gourd.
The Arhat has shed the dust and defilements of the sense-bases and transcended all realms of existence; how could he be the same as ordinary weeds?
He has silenced the three-inch tongue of the monk and displayed his spiritual powers within his almsbowl.

Welcoming Shancai back to the quiet chambers of the ancient Nanlou Temple, we closed the door together. Having met, we both ceased our formal practice and returned home. In these difficult times, we could do no more than share the same hearth;
do not believe the idle rumors of those who speak of right and wrong.
Chan Master Chang’s lotus-leaf robe was encountered by Master Zhao;
meeting things as they were, he upheld the ancestral wind. His tattered garment was left behind in a pool:
the autumn wind blew it apart, the spring wind mended it, without violating the single thread of the clear waves.
I pay homage at the stupa of Chan Master Zhao;
I recall the days of following the stream. Returning once more for this visit, at the very moment we meet upon crossing the threshold, there is no violation of the waves and tides at all.
Visiting Master Kong-sou of the Eastern Hall at Yuwang Monastery, we conversed late into the night.

After our illnesses had subsided, we sat facing one another like two withered stumps. Our frost-white hair hung in wisps, reflected against the warm window. Though there were brushes and ink to paint it, it could not be captured;
in the end, six times six do not make a pair.
Because of speaking of the many years of worn-out straw sandals, the patriarch thrust his feet in and forced them into place. From this point on, they became a chaotic mess with no bottom;
as one attempts to maintain them in order, they only become more discordant.
Worshipping the stupa of Chan Master Mian-’an:
wrapping a blade in cotton makes it difficult to approach; medicine within the rice comes from the Min region. To this day, people fear drinking the water of the mountains;
in the past, I once suffered the injury of poisoned insects.
Offering rice to Chan Master Fozhao:
it cannot be formed into a ball, nor can it be scattered apart. With one blow, all traces of the finest dust are severed.
From then on, through many subsequent festivals, they have all leaped forth before the winnowing basket.
I visited Master Songyuan of Xiangshan at his final abode;
he laughed at himself, saying, "How truly refined! Why must one be so intoxicated that one clings to the cup? At the crossroads stands a shop of wild weeds;
it has drawn people back and forth two or three times."
Master Xie Wuyong bestowed these shoes;
with my own hands I fashioned them, regardless of their length. A single thread secretly passes through the center. Looking at them, they are simply those of old;
having put them on, what hinders me from traveling everywhere?
Seeing off Zen Master Zhe-weng as he departs for Jing Mountain:
The ancient path is as slippery as moss; the patch-robed monk forgets his old steps. Coming from Tiantai, he now departs to dwell at Jing Mountain.
Family disgrace is broadcast abroad; raw iron is eaten by worms. A withered flower from a past season is blown by the wind into a verse for seeing off a traveler.
Sent to Master Monk Jieme: "In old age you hide like a tiger; it is difficult to deceive even a single person. Entering the forest is easy; climbing the tree is extremely difficult."
A thousand ravines beneath the tongue; ten thousand folds of mountains between the brows. For many years they have been pulled, yet they do not move;
the weeds grow ever more stubborn and dull. Sent from Master Gao Yuan of Ruiyan in Taizhou to Lingyin:
"The water emerges from the high plateau; its source is deep, reaching Cold Spring. Those who drink it find their tongues gone bald; those who smell it find their nostrils pierced through."
Both mouth and nose are lost; wondrous function transcends the biased and the orthodox. Tilting the ear and beckoning with the hand—listening to the ape, one calls out to the ape.
Amidst the shadows of creeping vines, the rocks lie piled high; two mountain streams merge, their ripples flowing on. Those coming from the south and those from the north pass beneath one’s feet;
if you wish to know the warmth or the cold, wait for a donkey-year.
Finding a path amidst the summer weeds within the hermitage, he conceals his form; he does not enter the herd of water-buffaloes in others' homes.
With a single snap of the fingers as a command, he bows his head in greeting with profound sincerity.
Enduring heavy sitting to sever isolation and peril, he refuses to rest; he bears the burden of magnificent pavilions and tiered towers.
The patriarch’s livelihood is as weighty as a mountain, yet his mastery is entirely returned to the crown of his head.

Living in the mountains, I have returned in old age to my former secluded peaks. Alone I embrace the unstrung zither, for there is no one left to appreciate its sound. Facing the cool breeze in stillness, I play a single melody;
the chirping of crickets joins in concert with the green forest.
The livelihood of one dwelling in the mountains is used according to the season; in every encounter, one follows the ancient path.
Merely employing a little strength from one's own hands, one stirs the embers and the cauldron heats itself.
The morning sun pierces through the tattered robe;
smiling, one gazes at the garment upon the body. A severed cloud seems about to fly away, yet the morning sun suddenly meets it. The eye of the needle has already been penetrated.
Facing the moon, one completes the remaining sutra.
Waiting for the moon, he finished the incomplete sutra; where has its meaning ever truly been? He handed it over to a foolish child, who now holds the yellow leaves in his hand.
*The Recorded Sayings of Master Zuan of Yunju* (End).
[There are additionally two volumes of the Outer Collection, the woodblocks of which remain at the residence of High Road Officer Qian Yan of Donghu.]
